questions.stem: 第 26 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】O) alike
副词
【词性槽】主语 + ___ + have dreamed，插在主语与谓语间修饰整句
【依据】alike 作副词表"同样地、都"，强调三类人"都"做过此梦
前文列举 Authors, artists and children三类主体，alike 置于其后表"作家、艺术家和孩子
都一样（地做过这样的梦）"，呼应开篇"延续数百年的幻想"。

questions.stem: 第 27 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】D) struck
动词
【词性槽】it found itself ___ by an invasion，过去分词作宾补
【依据】be struck by 表"遭受、被袭击"，小岛被彩蛋"大军"侵袭
宾语是 an invasion of colored plastic eggs（彩蛋的"入侵/大举涌来"）。be struck by
（遭…袭击）与 invasion 呼应，"小岛发现自己被一场彩蛋入侵所袭"，生动且搭配地道。
【竞争词】G) overthrown overthrown 指"推翻（政权）"，对象错位
overthrow 用于推翻政府、制度，海岛被彩蛋"推翻"语义荒谬，与 invasion of eggs 不搭。

questions.stem: 第 28 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】L) delight
名词
【词性槽】to the ___ of 结构里，定冠词 the 后必跟名词
【依据】蛋里有玩具，孩子"非常高兴"，且 much to the delight of 是固定表达
下文给出原因 because the eggs contained toys——蛋里装着玩具，对孩子是大喜
事。"much to the delight of local children"（令当地孩子大喜）语义与搭配双双吻合。
【竞争词】F) quantity 语义不对，孩子的是"喜悦"不是"数量"
quantity 指数量，"令孩子非常数量的是"不通；且 much to the quantity of 不成立。
H) mess 感情色彩相反，mess 是后文市长用的贬义词
mess（烂摊子）是负面的，而这里说的是孩子因蛋里有玩具而开心，色彩相反。mess 留给第
33 空（this is a huge __(33)__）。
B) wildlife 语义不搭，且 wildlife 留给第 34 空
"令当地孩子野生动物"不通；wildlife 应填 cause serious problems for __(34)__。
J) human "令孩子人类的"语义不成立
human 在此既不能表达孩子的情绪反应，也不与 much to the ... of 框架搭配。

questions.stem: 第 29 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】C) suspect
动词
【词性槽】Police ___ the eggs came...，主语 Police 后缺谓语
【依据】警方"猜测"蛋来自一艘失货货轮，suspect + 从句表推测
下文 the eggs came from a freighter that lost part of its cargo是警方推断的内容；
suspect that... 正表"警方怀疑/认为……"，符合警方调查口吻。

questions.stem: 第 30 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】I) intense
形容词
【词性槽】an unusually ___ storm，副词 + 空 + 名词，空作定语修饰 storm
【依据】形容"风暴"且后文"自2006年以来最猛"印证其强烈
同句下文 the worst to hit Germany's northeastern coast since 2006——自 2006 年以
来最严重的一场。an unusually intense storm（异常猛烈的风暴）与"最严重"互相印证。
【竞争词】M) colorful 搭配荒谬，"多彩的风暴"不通，且 colorful 留给第 32 空
colorful 形容色彩，修饰 storm 不合常理；它对应 everything was so __(32)__说蛋的缤纷。
K) effective "有效的风暴"语义不成立
effective 多修饰方法、手段，与 storm 不搭。
E) similar "相似的风暴"无所指，且缺被比较对象
similar 需有比较对象，且"异常相似的风暴"逻辑空洞，与"最严重"的语境不符。

questions.stem: 第 31 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】A) wore
动词
【词性槽】the joy ___ off soon，主语 joy 后缺谓语，紧跟 off
【依据】wear off 是固定短语"逐渐消退"，喜悦"很快消退"合转折
前句 "The surprise eggs have found their way to freedom"是欢快的，紧接 However,
the joy of the moment __(31)__ off soon——However 转折，"那一刻的喜悦很快消
退"。wore off（wear off 过去式）正表"渐渐消失"。
【竞争词】D) struck strike off 不表"消退"，与 joy 搭配不当
struck 与 off 不构成"喜悦消退"之义，且语义上"喜悦击落"不通；wear off 才是"（感觉）逐渐
消失"的地道搭配。

questions.stem: 第 32 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】M) colorful
形容词
【词性槽】everything was so ___，系动词 was + so + 空作表语
【依据】回指前文"彩色塑料蛋"，市长起初觉得"一切如此缤纷"像奇迹
前文 an invasion of colored plastic eggs——彩色塑料蛋遍地。市长说 At first I thought
this was a wonder, because everything was so __(32)__，"起初以为是奇迹，因为一切都
那么缤纷"，colorful 正回指那些彩蛋。
【竞争词】K) effective "一切都那么有效"与"奇迹"语境不搭
effective 形容功效，无法解释为何"像个奇迹"，也不回指彩蛋画面。
E) similar "一切都那么相似"语义突兀，缺比较对象
similar 需比较对象，"so similar"在"奇迹"的惊叹语境里说不通。

questions.stem: 第 33 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】H) mess
名词
【词性槽】a huge ___，冠词 a + 形容词 huge + 空，空作中心名词
【依据】but then 转折后揭示是个"大麻烦/烂摊子"
句中 but then we realized that this is a huge __(33)__ in the end——"但随后我们意识
到这最终是个大麻烦"。but then 与前半"以为是奇迹"对立，需一个负面名词，mess（烂摊
子）正合。
【竞争词】F) quantity 中性词，撑不起 but then 的负面转折
a huge quantity（大量）只表数量，无负面色彩，无法与"以为是奇迹"形成"喜→忧"的对立。
J) human "一个巨大的人类"语义不通
human 作可数名词指"一个人"，"a huge human"在此荒谬。
【易错】最具迷惑性的错误词是 F) —— quantity 也是名词、a huge quantity 看着也通，易忽略
色彩。this is a huge __(33)__ in the end 中 a huge quantity（大量）语法通顺，易被
选；防坑：but then 要求负面转折，quantity 中性、无法与前半"奇迹"对立，必须用贬义
的 mess。

questions.stem: 第 34 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】B) wildlife
名词
【词性槽】介词 for 后接宾语，需名词
【依据】塑料袋等垃圾对"野生动物"造成危害，环保语境最贴
上文 the plastic bags and other materials that have washed ashore——冲上岸的塑料
袋等垃圾。海洋塑料垃圾危害的正是 wildlife（野生动物），逻辑顺理成章。
【竞争词】J) human 义近干扰：垃圾确也害人，但本句焦点是海岛生态而非人
human 看着也沾边，但塑料垃圾在环保叙事里的典型受害者是野生动物；且全文未展开"对人的
危害"，选 wildlife 更贴文本，不靠常识硬推。
F) quantity "对数量造成问题"语义不通
problems for quantity 不成立，quantity 不是危害的承受方。
H) mess "对烂摊子造成问题"逻辑不通
mess 不是被危害的对象；且它将用于第 33 空。
【易错】最具迷惑性的错误词是 J) —— human 词性也对、常识上"垃圾害人"也通，最易误选。
cause serious problems for __(34)__ 里 human 与 wildlife 语法皆可、生活常识还偏
向"害人"；防坑：紧扣本段海岛环保焦点，文本说的是塑料垃圾对野生动物的危害，选贴文
本的 wildlife，不靠常识硬推。

questions.stem: 第 35 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】N) bore
动词
【词性槽】They ___ notes...，主语 They 后缺谓语，带宾语 notes
【依据】蛋"带有/装着"远方的纸条，bore（bear 过去式）表携带
上文 all these little eggs contained an extra treat with their toys说蛋里还藏着额外惊
喜。承接此意，They bore notes from afar——"它们带着来自远方的纸条"，bore 取
bear"携带、装载"义，与 contained 呼应。
【竞争词】A) wore wore 指"穿戴"，蛋"穿着纸条"不通
wore（wear 过去式）用于穿衣戴饰，与 notes 不搭；它对应第 31 空的 wore off。
D) struck struck 是"击中"，"击中纸条"语义荒谬
strike 表击打、袭击，不能与 notes 构成"带有纸条"之义。

title: 2023年03月真题·第1套 · 长篇匹配（Hyphenating your last na）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Congratulations on deciding to get married! While being married is great and wonderful, the act of getting married can be quite stressful. There is the planning of the ceremony itself, the merging(合并) of two households and all of the details involved in that. You also have to take the time to apply for your marriage license and then decide whether or not you are going to keep your last name or change it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This is where a lot of people have trouble. Once upon a time, it was just customary for a bride to take her groom's last name as her own and abandon her maiden name completely. The act of keeping her own last name was considered taboo(禁忌) and people's eyebrows would raise right off their faces when they found out that the bride was even considering something so radical. Over time, though, more and more women are deciding to keep their last names.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There are a lot of reasons to want to keep your own last name. Hopefully you have a supportive groom who understands why this idea is the most appealing to you. A lot of times, though, the act of keeping your name is still something that causes concern. Even if your groom is fine with it, his family (or your own) might not be so understanding.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are a couple of ways to compromise on the issue. You could choose an entirely new last name for the two of you to share. This way neither of you gets "your" way and you both have to deal with the legalities of going through a name change. Most of the time, though, the most popular compromise is to hyphenate your last name and the last name of your groom. For example, if your groom's name is John Smith and your name is Kate Jones, you would name yourself Kate Jones-Smith or Kate Smith-Jones. This allows you to keep going by your own last name while legally adopting your husband's last name at the same time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The compromise is the biggest reason that so many women choose to hyphenate their last names. It is a way of you keeping your own identity while also making your future husband happy. It allows you to stay connected to accomplishments that you achieved before you got married. For example, many women who choose to hyphenate do so partially because they have earned higher educational degrees and certifications under their maiden names. They might have also had things published or publicized and want to stay connected to that identity. Hyphenating your last name can help you bridge the gap between your personal and professional lives. Many women who opt to simply keep their own names do so because they don't want to give up all that they have accomplished professionally. Adopting their husband's last name makes it hard for them to claim ownership of these accomplishments personally because they happened under their "other" name.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: While tradition is one thing, there isn't any logical reason to completely change your name. Keeping your name and joining it to your husband's through hyphenation is as legal as simply adopting his name or as simply keeping your own and leaving his out of the picture entirely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Probably the most important reason to consider hyphenation is your identity. You've spent your whole life building your identity under a certain name. Obviously you will still be you even if you've taken on your husband's last name and omitted yours entirely. At the same time, your name is associated with the identity you've built up and hyphenation allows you to respect that while also respecting tradition and your husband's family's identity.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: If you care about outside opinions on your name, you should know that a large portion of today's society is annoyed by the hyphenated name. Some people find it "snobby"(势利的) and others simply find it irritating because they have a hard time remembering which last name they are supposed to say first. Some people even believe that not simply adopting your husband's last name is a huge sign of disrespect and a lack of commitment.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: It is possible that your future husband will find this choice offensive. Some men, regardless of how you might feel about such things, are traditionalists and feel that it is simply "right" for the woman to take the man's last name as her own. Whether your future husband insisting on your adopting his last name is a red flag to you or not, it is still something that you should take into consideration.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: There are all sorts of reasons to hyphenate your name or not to hyphenate your name. The basis for each of these things, however, is whether or not you are willing to make a compromise when it comes to changing your name. The hyphenation is the epitome(体现) of a compromise. One spouse wants a complete name change. The other spouse wants no name change. Hyphenating the two names is a way for each person to, at least a little bit, "win" the argument.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: And don't forget the legal stuff! Making the decision is just part of the process. From there you are going to have to legally change your name all over the place. You'll need to change your name at the bank, with social security, with your credit cards, on your driver's license, at the gym…everywhere. It's easy to get overwhelmed just thinking about it.

paragraphs.label: L
paragraphs.text: What matters, of course, is that the two of you are going to be happily married—hopefully for the rest of your lives. At the end of the day, whether you each keep your names, whether you come up with an entirely new name for the two of you to share or whether you hyphenate your current last names, what matters is that you love each other and are going to be joining your lives together. Try to remember that as you are staring at the application for your marriage license and filling out the portion that reads "name after you get married" (or whatever the legalese for that might be).

title: 2023年03月真题·第1套 · 仔细阅读 Passage 1

paragraphs.text: It's good to be smart. After all, intelligent people earn more money, accumulate more wealth, and even live longer. But there's another side to the story. The brightest people and strongest leaders sometimes make errors others don't, especially in situations that require common sense.

Travis Bradberry, president at TalentSmart, explained in his post Why Smart People Act So Stupid that "Rational thinking and intelligence don't tend to go hand in hand. Intelligent people are more prone to silly mistakes because of blind spots in how they use logic. These blind spots exist because smart people tend to be overconfident in their reasoning abilities." They are so used to being right and having quick answers that they don't even realise when they're making a mess by answering without thinking things through.

A lifetime of praise leads smart people to develop too much faith in their intelligence and abilities. They often fail to recognise when they need help, and when they do recognise it, they tend to believe that no one else is capable of providing it.

"It's hard for anyone to graciously accept the fact that they're wrong. It's even harder for smart people because they grow so used to being right all the time that it becomes a part of their identity," Bradberry wrote. "For smart people, being wrong can feel like a personal attack, and being right, a necessity."

Smart people also have a hard time accepting feedback. They tend to undervalue the opinions of others, which means they have trouble believing that anyone is qualified to give them useful feedback. Not only does this tendency hinder their growth and performance, it can lead to harmful relationships, both personally and professionally.

Smart people develop overachieving personalities because things come so easily to them. They simply don't understand how hard some people have to work to accomplish the same things, and because of that, they push people too hard. They set the bar too high, and when people take too long or don't get things quite right, they assume it's due to a lack of effort. So they push even harder.

questions.stem: What do we learn from the passage about the brightest people?

options.label: B
options.text: They usually turn a blind eye to their own weaknesses.

options.label: C
options.text: They are admired by people around them.

options.label: D

questions.explanation:
【答案】A （细节题）
【判型】题干 What do we learn from the passage about the brightest people? 是开放式问 "关
于聪明人我们知道了什么"，没有 infer/imply 之类的推断信号，也不问主旨或态度——属
于覆盖全篇的细节判断题。
【拆句】What do we learn from the passage about the brightest people? 主干是 what do we
learn，about the brightest people 是后置介词短语修饰 learn 的内容范围；结构平铺直
叙，无陷阱。
【定位】The brightest people and strongest leaders sometimes make errors others don't, especially in
situations that require common sense.
最聪明的人和最强的领导者有时会犯别人不会犯的错，尤其是在那些需要常识的场合。
【选项】A) ✓ 正确
make errors others don't, especially in situations that require common sense ↔
make silly mistakes in straightforward situations
They can make silly mistakes in straightforward situations. 把预判的 "在常识场景中
犯错" 完整复现，且与定位句逐成分对应，是定位句的同义替换。
B) 无中生有
文章只说聪明人有 blind spots in how they use logic，并没有说他们对 "自己的弱点
视而不见"——turn a blind eye to their own weaknesses 是凭文字面感受瞎想出来的
关联。
C) 无中生有
文章只提到 intelligent people earn more money, accumulate more wealth, and
even live longer，没说他们被人 "敬仰"——admired by people around them 属原文
未提的事实陈述。
D) 答非所问
末段确实提到 Smart people develop overachieving personalities，但全文聚焦的是
聪明人的共性问题，并未论述他们 "个性各异"——differ in their personalities 与文章
问的 "我们了解到什么" 不在一个频道。

questions.stem: How do smart people react when they are found to be wrong?

options.label: A

"被发现错了"，问对应反应，是定位到具体段落求证的细节题。

people react，when 引导时间状语从句限定情境；从句用被动语态 are found to be

【定位】For smart people, being wrong can feel like a personal attack, and being right, a necessity.
对聪明人来说，被认定为错可以感觉像一次人身攻击，而正确则是一种必需。
【选项】A) 过度推断

paragraphs.text: Of the endless troubles that come with being driven from one's home country, losing educational certificates may seem small. But it isn't. Refugees who settle in other countries often find themselves unable to continue on their previous career path due to a new set of employer standards or skills requirements. To solve this problem, the U.S. State Department is posing a solution: online learning.

The State Department will announce a partnership with an online education platform called Coursera. The platform will allow refugees worldwide to take thousands of online courses for free. "Coursera for Refugees" will be available for any non-profit group that supports refugees in any country, as well as individual refugees. They can apply for fully funded access to Coursera's course catalog, which means they can take all of the platform's classes and obtain professional certificates for free. The platform currently offers professor-led lectures on a broad range of topics, from data science to fashion design.

As the world migrant crisis intensifies, employment is becoming a global concern. The new program aims to aid refugees by offering "important skills that will help them in the global economy," Evan Ryan, U.S. assistant secretary of state for educational and cultural affairs, said on a press call last week. "What we don't want to do is not act," added Coursera chief operations officer Lila Ibrahim.

The idea isn't without problems. For one, starting a new career path isn't as simple as watching a few videos and obtaining an online certificate; even those looking to continue previous careers can't simply rely on an online lecture to get them up-to-date on standards, policies, and practices. For another, most of the classes on Coursera are in English, and though there are plans to add translations, language barriers can be a big obstacle. Then there are the questions over the value of massive open online courses (MOOCs) themselves—both for refugees and for average learners.
But it's still early days and there are signs of hope. In 2015, a joint study found 72% of people taking the MOOCs saw career benefits afterwards.

questions.stem: Why is the U.S. State Department launching an online learning program for refugees?

options.label: A
options.text: To enable them to settle down in host countries.

options.label: B
options.text: To allow them to learn as many job skills as possible.

options.label: C
options.text: To offer them a platform to pursue advanced degrees.

options.label: D
options.text: To help them to meet new employment standards.

questions.explanation:
【答案】D （细节题）
【判型】Why is the U.S. State Department launching an online learning program for
refugees?问的是一个具体的发起原因，答案应能在原文中明确找到对应句。
【拆句】Why is the U.S. State Department launching an online learning program for
refugees?是一个 Why 引导的现在进行时疑问句，主语是机构名，介词短语for refugees点
明服务对象，结构平铺、无陷阱。
【定位】Refugees who settle in other countries often find themselves unable to continue on their
previous career path due to a new set of employer standards or skills requirements. To solve
this problem, the U.S. State Department is posing a solution: online learning.
在他国安顿的难民常常发现，自己因雇主新一套的标准或技能要求而无法延续原来的职业路
径。为解决这个问题，美国国务院正在推出一个方案：在线学习。
【选项】A) 偷换概念：把前提说成目的
To enable them to settle down in host countries.把项目目的说成帮助难民「在东道
国安顿下来」，但原文中settle in other countries是难民已经发生的状态、是项目的前
提，不是项目的目的。
B) 过度推断：拔高程度词
To allow them to learn as many job skills as possible.把目的扩成「学尽可能多的工
作技能」，而原文目的是「应对一套新的雇主标准」，原文并没有用「尽可能多」这类
极端量词。
C) 偷换概念：证书↔学位
To offer them a platform to pursue advanced degrees.把目的说成「追求高等学
位」，但原文第二段说的是obtain professional certificates，是专业证书而非学位。
D) ✓ 正确
a new set of employer standards or skills requirements ↔ new employment standards
To solve this problem, the U.S. State Department is posing a solution ↔ To help them to meet
预判答案是「帮助难民应对他国雇主的新标准」，与To help them to meet new
employment standards.在主语、动作、对象、目的状语上四点全部对应，是唯一与定
位句构成同义替换的选项。

questions.stem: What do we know about "Coursera for Refugees"?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides refugees with a wide range of courses free of charge.

options.label: B
options.text: It offers free online data services for refugees around the world.

options.label: C
options.text: It allows refugees to obtain degrees in various academic fields.

options.label: D
options.text: It supplies refugees with a great variety of job opportunities.

questions.explanation:
【答案】A （细节题）
【判型】What do we know about "Coursera for Refugees"?要求选出关于该项目可以确认的事
实，属于客观信息核对。
【拆句】What do we know about "Coursera for Refugees"?结构非常简单，主句是What do we
know，介词宾语就是引号里的专名，无干扰修饰。
【定位】They can apply for fully funded access to Coursera's course catalog, which means they can
take all of the platform's classes and obtain professional certificates for free. The platform
currently offers professor-led lectures on a broad range of topics, from data science to
fashion design.
他们可以申请由项目全额资助的Coursera课程目录访问权限，这意味着他们可以免费修读该
平台的所有课程并获得专业证书。该平台目前提供由教授主讲的讲座，主题广泛，从数据科
学到时装设计。
【选项】A) ✓ 正确
a broad range of topics ↔ a wide range of courses
for free ↔ free of charge
预判要求「免费+各种各样的课」，It provides refugees with a wide range of
courses free of charge.在主语、动作、对象、范围、付费方式上五点齐备，是定位句
最干净的同义复述。
B) 偷换概念：把举例项当成核心
It offers free online data services for refugees around the world.把项目说成「提供
免费在线数据服务」，但原文from data science to fashion design中的 data science
只是众多课程主题之一，不是项目所提供的服务内容。
C) 偷换概念：证书↔学位再现
It allows refugees to obtain degrees in various academic fields.说项目能让难民拿
到「各学术领域的学位」，但原文是professional certificates——专业证书而非学位，
也没有强调「学术领域」。
D) 无中生有：用近义类比制造跳跃
It supplies refugees with a great variety of job opportunities.把项目说成提供「多
种多样的工作机会」，但原文从头到尾说的是「课程」与「证书」，不是「工作」。

questions.stem: What does the passage say is a consequence of the global migrant crisis?

options.label: C
options.text: A lot more refugees die during migration.

options.label: D
options.text: Refugees find it more difficult to get a job.

questions.explanation:
【答案】D （细节题）
【判型】What does the passage say is a consequence of the global migrant crisis?直接问「文
章说……的后果是什么」，答案应能在原文明确找到。
【拆句】What does the passage say is a consequence of the global migrant crisis?是
「What+助动词+主语+谓语+从句宾语」的疑问句，从句is a consequence of...提示答案
的逻辑位置是后果一端，结构平铺。
【定位】As the world migrant crisis intensifies, employment is becoming a global concern.
随着全球移民危机加剧，就业正成为全球性的关切。
【选项】A) 过度推断：从一点滑向全局
Instability increases in host countries.说东道国整体不稳定上升，但原文只说就业一
项成为全球关切，并未提社会稳定层面。
B) 张冠李戴：动词从一个主语挪到另一个主语
The global economic crisis intensifies.说全球经济危机加剧，但原文只说就业问题，
不是「经济危机」；intensifies 在原文里是用来形容 migrant crisis 的，不是
economic crisis。
C) 无中生有：用常识联想替代文本
A lot more refugees die during migration.说更多难民死于迁徙途中，但原文从头到
尾没有涉及死亡话题，属典型无中生有。
D) ✓ 正确
employment is becoming a global concern ↔ Refugees find it more difficult to get a job
a global concern ↔ more difficult
预判结论是「就业难度上升」，本篇主体始终是难民，Refugees find it more difficult
to get a job.既保留了主体，又把抽象的「关切」落地到「找工作变难」，是唯一与定
位句因果直接对应的选项。
questions.locateHint: As the world migrant crisis intensifies, employment is becoming a global concern.

【答案】C （细节题）
【判型】What does the author say causes refugees' difficulty in taking online courses?问的是
「作者说」的具体原因，回原文找归因句即可。
【拆句】What does the author say causes refugees' difficulty in taking online courses?主干是
What causes ... difficulty，does the author say是插入语，in taking online courses做后
置定语限定 difficulty，结构稍绕但无陷阱。
【定位】For another, most of the classes on Coursera are in English, and though there are plans to add
translations, language barriers can be a big obstacle.
另一方面，Coursera上的大多数课程都是英文授课，尽管有添加翻译的计划，语言障碍仍可
能是一个大问题。
【选项】A) 无中生有：用相关话题替换原文话题
Cultural environment.把困难归因到「文化环境」，但原文第四段从未涉及文化差异，
是无中生有。
B) 张冠李戴：把另一困难的原因装到本题
Changed academic requirements.想说的是「学术要求改变」，但原文can't simply
rely on an online lecture to get them up-to-date on standards, policies, and
practices说的是行业「标准、政策、做法」的更新，而非学术要求；且这是第一条困
难，不是题54问的「上网课的困难原因」，而是「换行业的困难」。
C) ✓ 正确
language barriers can be a big obstacle ↔ Lack of language skills
most of the classes on Coursera are in English ↔ Lack of language skills
预判明确指向「语言」，四个选项中只有Lack of language skills.提及语言；与定位句
构成最干净的因果对应。
D) 偷换概念：把对一物的质疑换成多物之差异
Difference in teaching platforms.说困难是「教学平台之间的差异」，但原文there
are the questions over the value of massive open online courses (MOOCs)
themselves谈的是对MOOCs整体价值的质疑，不是不同平台之间的差异。

questions.stem: What did the joint study find about the MOOCs several years ago?

options.label: A
options.text: They helped solve learners' financial problems.

options.label: B
options.text: They benefited most of the learners.

options.label: C
options.text: They changed some learners' career path.

options.label: D
options.text: They provided the most needed vocational skills.

questions.explanation:
【答案】B （细节题）
【判型】What did the joint study find about the MOOCs several years ago?问一个具体研究的
具体发现，是直白的事实核对。
【拆句】What did the joint study find about the MOOCs several years ago?是过去时一般疑问
句，主语the joint study，宾语为 what，时间状语several years ago提示要找过去时句
子，结构平铺。
【定位】In 2015, a joint study found 72% of people taking the MOOCs saw career
benefits afterwards.
2015年，一项联合研究发现，参加MOOCs课程的人中有72%在之后获得了职业上的益处。
【选项】A) 偷换概念：用常识把「职业」换成「财务」
They helped solve learners' financial problems.说MOOCs帮学习者解决「财务问
题」，但原文只说career benefits——职业益处，不是钱。
B) ✓ 正确
72% of people taking the MOOCs ↔ most of the learners
saw career benefits afterwards ↔ benefited
预判结论是「大多数学习者获益」，They benefited most of the learners.在主语、动
词、对象上三点对应——只是用程度词代替数字、用动词代替名词短语，是最干净的同
义改写。
C) 过度推断：把益处程度拔高到根本改变
They changed some learners' career path.说MOOCs「改变了某些学习者的职业路
径」，但原文只说saw career benefits——获得职业益处，从「获益」到「改变路径」
是过度推断。
D) 过度推断+无中生有：加最高级、加具体内容
They provided the most needed vocational skills.说MOOCs提供「最需要的职业技
能」，但原文只笼统说「职业益处」，并未说提供了什么具体技能，更没有「最需要」
这种最高级。

title: 2022年12月真题·第3套 · 选词填空

paragraphs.text: Phones influence all aspects of teenage life. Ninety-five percent of Americans ages 13 to 17 have a smartphone or have access to one, and nearly half report using the internet "almost  [26]  ."

But as recent survey data and interviews have suggested, many teens find much of that time to be unsatisfyingly spent. Continuous  [27]  shouldn't be mistaken for endless enjoyment. A new  [28]  representative survey about "screen time and device distractions" from the Pew Research Center indicates that it's not just parents who think teenagers are worryingly  [29]  from their phones—many teens themselves do too. Fifty-four percent of the 13- to 17-year-olds surveyed said they spend too much time  [30]  in their phones.

Vicky Rideout, who runs a research firm that studies children's interactions with media and technology, was not surprised by this finding. She says it's hardly  [31]  to teenagers. "They are dealing with the same challenges that adults are, as far as they are living in the  [32]  of a tech environment designed to suck as much of their time onto their devices as possible," Rideout says.

The way parents interact with technology can  [33]  the way they interact with their kids. Rideout thus thinks it's up to parents to model good  [34]  : Kids tend to take note if their parents put their phone away at dinner or charge it in another room while they sleep. Witnessing habits like that can help kids "realize that they can  [35]  some more control over their devices," she says.

title: 2022年12月真题·第3套 · 长篇匹配（Evil Genius）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A few years ago I found myself teaching a university class on evil. It was for third-year criminology students to help them contextualize theory and research within controversial current topics. It was a huge success. The debates were heated and interesting. I could see people's views change within the course of a single lecture. Over the past 13 years, as a student, lecturer and researcher, I've enjoyed discussing the science of evil with anyone willing to listen. What I like most is destroying the cliche(陈词滥调) of good and evil, and replacing them with scientific insight. We need a more informed way of discussing behavior that at first we cannot, or should not, begin to understand.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Without understanding, we risk dehumanizing others, writing off human beings simply because we don't comprehend them. We must try to understand what we have labeled evil. We tend to think evil is something that other people are. We think of ourselves as "good people", and even when we do morally wrong things, we understand the context of our decisions. With others, however, it is far easier to write them off. If their actions deviate(偏离) substantially from what we consider acceptable, we may label them evil. We need to be careful with this. Calling someone evil is often similar to saying they cannot change, and perhaps aren't even a human at all. However, when you actually go monster-hunting, and you look deeply at the people behind shocking behavior, you may be surprised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: As a child I used to love the Scooby-Doo cartoons. Arriving in their "Mystery Machine", the gang would have to find a monster who was terrorizing a neighborhood. They would run around looking for clues and at the end unmask the bad guy. It was always a normal person in a costume. There were no monsters. Like the Scooby crew, we may find ourselves hunting for an easy fix, one word for people who do bad things. But if we take a good look, the word "evil" is insufficient—there are no simple explanations for why humans do bad things: instead there are many, and they are all marvelously different.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evil is typically referred to when there is deviance from social norms: formal deviance is the violation of laws, like theft, murder, and attacks, while informal deviance involves violations of social norms, like lying. Evil behavior is typically thought to embrace one or both forms. However, deviance can also describe a behavior that simply differs from the norm.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps this is where we can find the good side of our bad side. Deviating from the norm can make us villains(恶棍), but it can also make us heroes. A child deviates from social pressures when they stand up for another child being bullied in school. A soldier deviates when they choose not to follow orders to kill an innocent civilian. An employee in a big tech company deviates when they expose its wrongdoings.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Creativity is also a deviation. Here, too, things are complex. Thinking creatively has given us modern medicine, technology and modern political structures, but it has also given us poison and nuclear weapons. Great benefit and great harm can come from the same human tendency.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In a research paper, Evil Genius, published in 2014, the behavioral scientists Francesca Gino and Scott Wiltermuth wanted to examine whether people who behave unethically in one task are more creative than others on a subsequent task, even after controlling for differences in baseline creative skills. The unethical behavior they chose was dishonesty.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Over five experiments, researchers gave participants tasks in which they could cheat. In one study, they were given matrices(矩阵) and had to find two numbers that added up to 10. Participants were asked to self-report how well they did at the end of the study: 59% cheated by saying that they solved more matrices than they actually had.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: After each task, the researchers measured participants' performance on the Remote Associates Test. This shows participants three words at a time that appear to be unrelated, and the person has to think of a fourth word that is associated with all of them. For example, you might get "Fox, Man, Peep", or "Dust, Cereal, Fish". In order to find the linking words ("Hole" for the first, "Bowl" for the second) you need to be creative. The more you get right, the more creative you are thought to be because you have come up with uncommon associations.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: For every one of the five studies, they found the same thing—participants who cheated in the first task did better on the creativity task. Why? Like other forms of unethical behavior, lying means breaking rules. It involves being deviant, going against the social principle that people should tell the truth. Similarly, being creative involves "thinking outside the box", deviating from expectations. They involve similar thought patterns, so stimulating one stimulates the other. Can we learn from this? Perhaps. To be more creative, we could try lying in a controlled environment. Find online logic games and cheat at them, play Scrabble(拼字游戏) with a dictionary, or write a story about something that is untrue? Such tasks can get our brains thinking flexibly, beyond our normal comfort zone. This is not a call to become a compulsive(强迫性的) liar, but a controlled liar.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: In addition to benefits for creativity, deviance can be a good thing in other ways. Even Philip Zimbardo, the author of the Stanford prison experiment, who showed how easily we can be led to behave badly, believes that the future of deviance research may lie more in understanding extreme pro-social behavior, such as heroism. Like evil, we often view heroism as only a possibility for outliers—for people who are abnormal. But Zimbardo asks: "What if the capability to act heroically is also fundamentally ordinary and available to all of us?" Some say we should never meet our heroes, lest they disappoint us when we find out how normal they are. But this should be liberating, not disappointing. We are all capable of behaving like outliers. It's time for us to understand deviance, and realize its potential for good as well as for harm.

title: 2022年12月真题·第3套 · 仔细阅读 Passage 1

paragraphs.text: Even though we are living in an age where growing old is thought of as an inevitable misery, this doctor has been changing the game for seniors over the last 25 years.

It all started in 1991 when the Harvard-educated physician was transferred from working in a stressful emergency room to being the medical director of a nursing home in upstate New York. The depressing and regimented(严格管制的) environment got him thinking on what exactly could improve the residents' conditions.

Even though animals in nursing homes were illegal at the time, Dr. Bill Thomas took a chance. Based on a hunch(直觉), he brought in two dogs, four cats, hens, rabbits, 100 birds, a multitude of plants, a flower garden, and a vegetable patch.
The change was dramatic. There was a 50% drop in medical prescriptions along with a dramatic decrease in death rates—but most importantly, the residents were simply happier.

Dr. Thomas's approach, named the Eden Alternative, has driven nursing homes to allow a more autonomous(自主的) and creative living space for their elderly. It erases the belief that growing old means growing useless. He encourages residents to think of their age as an enriching new phase of life rather than the end of it.

Thomas, now a speaker and author of several books, also created small, independently-run residences with their own bedrooms and bathrooms, and he has been preaching a singular message that getting old is not a bad thing.

"Within six weeks, they had to send a truck around to pick up all the wheelchairs," Thomas told the Washington Post. "You know why most people in nursing homes use wheelchairs? Because the buildings are so big."

The 56-year-old doctor's methods have been adopted in Australia, Japan, Canada, and America with enormous success. Last year he published Second Wind: Navigating the Passage to a Slower, Deeper, and More Connected Life, a guide on how to shift our perspectives on aging and growth.
He is currently traveling through North America performing with his guitar and his enthusiasm on his Age of Disruption Tour.

title: 2022年12月真题·第3套 · 仔细阅读 Passage 2

paragraphs.text: Research shows that in developed countries, more affluent and educated people tend to consume higher-quality diets—including more fruits and vegetables, fish and whole grains. On the contrary, economically disadvantaged people report diets that are nutrient-poor and energy-dense. They are less likely to have food-purchasing habits that conform to public health recommendations.

These dietary differences are often accompanied by higher rates of obesity and diabetes among lower-income people. This relationship between social class and diet quality and health is extensively documented. However, the research does not explain why this is the case—a question that has significant implications for designing effective policies and initiatives to improve diets and prevent chronic diseases.

Public-health initiatives to promote healthy diets often focus on providing nutrition education and recipes(食谱). These approaches, however, often presume less food literacy (i.e., food knowledge and skills) among low-income people. Are unhealthy diets really the result of poor choices, limited food skills and knowledge?

Research suggests that adults in food-insecure households are just as likely as those in food-secure households to adjust recipes to make them more healthy. They are also just as proficient in food preparation and cooking skills. There is no indication that increasing food skills or budgeting skills will reduce food insecurity.

Instead, disadvantaged groups are constrained by their economic, material and social circumstances. For example, low income is the strongest predictor of food insecurity in Canada, where one in eight households experiences insufficient access to nutritious foods.

It's well-established that food prices are an important determinant of food choice. Low-income households report that they find it difficult to adopt dietary guidelines because food prices are a barrier to improving their diets.
When researchers estimate the cost of diets people actually eat, higher-quality diets are typically more costly.

While this may be so, it does not, in itself, prove that healthy diets are necessarily more expensive or cost-prohibitive. After all, not all socioeconomically disadvantaged people consume poor diets.
We can easily think of a number of foods and recipes that are both inexpensive and nutritious. The internet is full of recipes for "eating well on a budget."

paragraphs.text: Parenting brings fathers more joy than it does mothers, according to a new study. The research examined three studies  [26]  more than 18,000 participants. Across all three, parenthood was  [27]  with more positive wellbeing outcomes for dads than for mums.

So why are fathers happier than mothers? "Fathers may fare better than mothers in part due to how they spend time with their children," said lead author Katherine Nelson-Coffey. In one study, the authors  [28]  that dads were more likely to take "playing" as an  [29]  activity both when caring for their kids and spending time with their kids. "Playing with their children likely offers parents opportunities to experience positive feelings and  [30]  closeness with their children," they say.

Fathers also did better than men without kids, reporting greater happiness, life satisfaction, and fewer  [31]  symptoms. They also reported greater connectedness and autonomy(自主). For mums,  [32]  , compared to women without children, the results weren't quite as positive. Mums reported greater autonomy, but also "greater trouble" and fewer positive  [33]  .

Mums reported happier moods while interacting with their kids, compared to other experiences, but not while engaging  [34]  in childcare. "This difference suggests that how mothers and fathers spend time with their children might have important  [35]  for their wellbeing," the authors write. They suspect that mums may be less happy than dads because they're more likely to have higher expectations about parenthood. As such, they're more likely to be "let down" by the experience.

title: 2022年12月真题·第2套 · 长篇匹配（Learning to say no）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not doing something will always be faster than doing it. This philosophy applies in many areas of life. For example, there is no meeting that goes faster than not having a meeting at all. This is not to say you should never attend another meeting, but the truth is that we say "yes" to too many things we don't actually want to do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: How often do people ask you to do something and you just reply, "Sure." Three days later, you're overwhelmed by how much is on your to-do list. We become frustrated by our obligations even though we were the ones who said "yes" to them in the first place. Even worse, people will occasionally fight to do things that waste time. You don't have to do something just because it exists. It's worth asking if things are necessary. Many of them are not, and a simple "no" will be more productive than whatever work the most efficient person can cope with. But if the benefits of saying "no" are so obvious, then why do we say "yes" so often?

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: We say "yes" to many requests not because we want to do them, but because we don't want to be seen as rude or unhelpful. Often, we have to consider saying "no" to someone we will interact with again in the future—our co-worker, our spouse, our family and friends. Saying "no" to our superiors at work can be particularly difficult. In these situations, I like the approach recommended in Essentialism by Greg McKeown. He writes, "Remind your superiors what you would be neglecting if you said 'yes' and force them to deal with the trade-off. For example, if your manager comes to you and asks you to do X, you can respond with 'Yes, I'm happy to make this the priority. Which of these other projects should I deprioritize to pay attention to this new project?'"

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Collaborating with others is an important element of life. The thought of straining the relationship outweighs the commitment of our time and energy. For this reason, it can be helpful to be gracious in your response. Do whatever favors you can, and be warm-hearted and direct when you have to say no. But even after we have accounted for these social considerations, many of us still seem to do a poor job of managing the trade-off between yes and no. We find ourselves over-committed to things that don't meaningfully improve or support those around us, and certainly don't improve our own lives.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps one issue is how we think about the meaning of yes and no. The words "yes" and "no" get so often used in comparison with each other that it feels like they carry equal weight in conversation. In reality, they're not just opposite in meaning, but of entirely different magnitudes in commitment. When you say "no", you're only saying "no" to one option. When you say "yes", you're saying "no" to every other option. I like how economist Tim Harford put it, "Every time we say 'yes' to a request, we're also saying 'no' to anything else we might accomplish with the time?" Once you're committed to something, you've already decided how that future block of time will be spent. In other words, saying "no" saves you time in the future. Saying "yes" costs you time in the future. "No" is a form of time credit. You retain the ability to spend your future time however you want. "Yes" is a form of time debt. You have to pay back your commitment at some point.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: "No" is a decision. "Yes" is a responsibility. Saying "no" is sometimes seen as a luxury that only those in power can afford. And it's true: turning down opportunities is easier when you can fall back on the safety net provided by power, money, and authority. But it's also true that saying "no" is not merely a privilege reserved for the successful. It's also a strategy that can help you become successful. Saying "no" is an important skill to develop at any stage of your career because it retains the most important asset in life: your time. As investor Pedro Sorrentino put it, "If you don't guard your time, people will steal it from you." You need to say "no" to whatever isn't leading you toward your goals.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Nobody embodied this idea better than Steve Jobs, who said, "People think focus means saying 'yes' to the thing you've got to focus on. But that's not what it means at all. It means saying 'no' to the hundred other good ideas that there are. You have to pick carefully." Jobs had another great quote about saying "no": "I'm actually as proud of the things we haven't done as the things I have done. Innovation is saying 'no' to 1,000 things."

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Over time, as you continue to improve and succeed, your strategy needs to change. The opportunity cost of your time increases as you become more successful. At first, you just eliminate the obvious distractions and explore the rest. As your skills improve and you learn to separate what works from what doesn't, you have to continually increase your threshold for saying "yes". You still need to say "no" to distractions, but you also need to learn to say "no" to opportunities that were previously good uses of time, so you can make space for better uses of time. It's a good problem to have, but it can be a tough skill to master.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: What is true about health is also true about productivity: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. More effort is wasted doing things that don't matter than is wasted doing things inefficiently. And if that is the case, elimination is a more useful skill than optimization. I'm reminded of the famous Peter Drucker quote, "There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all."

title: 2022年12月真题·第2套 · 仔细阅读 Passage 1

paragraphs.text: We're eating more fish than ever these days. At around 20 kilograms per person global fish consumption is now more than twice what it was in the 1960s. What's really remarkable, though, is where that fish comes from.
For the first time in human history, most of our aquatic(水产的) food now comes from farming rather than fishing.

People ate around 73 million tonnes of farmed fish—just more than half of the volume of fish that humans consumed—in 2014. That's out of a total fish supply of 167 million tonnes; the remaining 20 million or so tonnes go into things like animal feed and medical products.
To keep eating fish at the current rate, we're definitely going to need to keep aquaculture(水产养殖) developing. That's because the volume of fish caught in the wild has leveled off since the 1990s.
Back in 1974, only 10% of marine fish stocks had been overfished. Now, more than three-tenths are. Only a tenth of our oceans' fish stocks could sustain heavier fishing than current levels.

But while catchings at sea have suffered, fish-farming has been growing at a fast rate. A lot of that is coming from China, which produces 60% of the world's farmed fish. In fact, some 35 countries, including China, now produce more farmed than wild-caught fish.

This shift toward aquaculture isn't just good for ensuring salmon(三文鱼) on your plate; it's also crucial to ensuring food security and sustainability. By 2050, the world will need to feed an estimated 9.7 billion people. They'll have to get their protein somewhere. However, raising cattle, pigs, and other land-based animals requires vast sums of grain and water. For example, pound for pound, beef requires 15 times more feed to raise than carp, a freshwater fish farmed all over Asia. That grain—and the water needed to grow it—could be consumed by people instead.

However, aquaculture is no silver bullet. In some southeast Asian countries, shrimp farming does disastrous damage to marine ecosystems. Despite these problems, however, shrimp continues to be among the most popular sea foods worldwide.

title: 2022年12月真题·第2套 · 仔细阅读 Passage 2

paragraphs.text: In 2020, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the World Food Programme (WFP).

Why a Nobel Prize for the WFP, and why now? In 2019, the WFP assisted nearly 100 million people in 88 countries. It is the safety net for those who fall off the edge of existence. It is a response to solving the problem of food instability. Its Nobel Prize reminds us all of the moral hazard in imagining that the poor and vulnerable are somebody else's problem.

The WFP has been around since 1961 and has been the global coordinator of nationally based efforts to avoid disasters with food aid. Despite decades of effort to eliminate hunger, the latest estimate is that about 11% of people on the planet (about 820 million people) are suffering daily undernourishment. Progress at reducing undernourishment has stopped despite gains through the 1990s and 2000s.

Developed countries sometimes offer food and aid to developing ones, but at a price. One American philosopher stated that addressing the needs of the poor and vulnerable is about more than money—it is mostly about creating conditions under which prosperity and opportunity can thrive. When aid is offered with heavy conditions attached, like loan repayment or food for resources, it often widens the gap between rich and poor and sustains the old world order. This is why the work of the WFP is so vital.

The scientific community, however, can provide a helping hand to the WFP. By sharing knowledge of agriculture and climate with peers in countries most vulnerable to poverty and hunger, scientists can help reduce these problems. By making its voice heard, science can lead by example. The ability to overcome food shortages that must be built into some of the poorest countries will not come from loans from wealthy countries, which may have food problems of their own, or world economic institutions. This ability will be built upon self-confident people using open and shared scientific knowledge to pull themselves out of their misery.

【拆句】主干是 What does ... make us realize，the WFP's winning of the Nobel Peace Prize 是
动名词短语作主语，winning 由所有格 the WFP's 修饰、of 短语补足对象；理解上等价

title: 2022年12月真题·第1套 · 长篇匹配（The hidden costs college）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: This fall, thousands of college students from across the country will begin their undergraduate studies at colleges around the nation. They will inevitably pack too much to fit in their tiny dorm rooms. They will also carry with them a huge student loan debt, in addition to countless "hidden" out-of-pocket costs paid for by their bank accounts and the bank accounts of their families.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At my well-respected, private, four-year university in Washington, D.C., which boasts a yearly tuition of $44,046 not including room and board, I receive over $57,000 yearly in financial aid. As a student from a family that is struggling to make ends meet, my financial aid package is a combination of federal grants and federal work study, university merit scholarships and financial aid awards, and about $8,000 yearly in federally subsidized(有补贴的) and unsubsidized loans. On paper, my expenses and my financial aid just about even out. Off paper, they don't.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Universities today are in the business of making money, and mine is no exception. They hit me right out of the gate with a $160 fee to attend my freshman orientation, a price which does not include the cost of travel to and from the District. Almost every class has an associated fee not included in the cost of tuition, most between $40 and $100. Fees for lab science classes are the highest, and all students at my university are required to take at least one lab before they graduate. Buying a laptop proved a necessity and, thankfully, a relative bought me one as a gift. Renting a mini-fridge for my dorm room costs my roommates and me about $140 a year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Schools will charge you whatever they can. The costs of any damage to the dorm, including elevators, bathrooms, and common areas, are billed to every person on a dorm floor, or even the entire building if they do not know who caused the damage. After I fell out of my bed twice during my freshman year, the university installed a railing—for $20, billed to my student account. My financial aid did not anticipate any of these costs, and so it did not cover them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An Internet search of "hidden costs" of college turns up a host of articles on parent-centered websites on the college application process. These articles are almost always geared towards upper- and middle-class families. For students already struggling to pay tuition, these costs may be the least of their worries.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: So what hidden costs should low-income students really be paying attention to? My college experience offers a few examples.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If you are a low-income student who will be attending school out-of-state, make sure you know if you can use your state benefits, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. It wasn't until after I had accepted admission to an out-of-state school that I learned that I could not use my Ohio Medicaid on campus for anything other than emergency care. My benefits became invalid the second I moved out of Ohio. After my freshman year, I had to opt for the school's insurance plan, which costs around $2,000 a year. Even if your school offers a flat-rate fee for a doctor's appointment at the student health center (mine is $20 a visit), these fees often do not include extra fees for lab tests or prescription medications(药物).

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: If you plan on paying off bills in your student account with a credit card, be aware of any additional costs. My school charges an additional fee for the use of a credit card to settle outstanding charges, which can add upwards of 3% of the balance to your bill.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: There is another depressing reality hidden within even the largest financial aid packages: Colleges often offer the most generous packages during freshman year as a way to attract new students. My family was careful to ask about the chances of financial aid being taken away after my freshman year. We were assured that, except for low grades or a raise in family income, no money would be taken away. We did not know to ask—and the school did not readily point out—that even if tuition rises, my financial aid package will stay the same. So when my university voted to raise tuition costs 3% at the end of my freshman year, my financial aid package remained the same and I was suddenly responsible for an additional $1,200 for the next year. The university administration will likely vote to raise costs at least once more before my graduation.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Yes, I chose to attend an expensive university far from my hometown. Yes, there were cheaper options. But there are promising students from struggling families across the nation who should not rule out their dream schools entirely. All things considered, I am paying significantly less than the ticket price of my university, and having an educational experience in Washington, D.C., that I would not have had anywhere else. As a low-income student from a down-and-out Rust Belt community, these educational experiences have enormous potential to brighten my future—and my family's future.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: The key is to make sure that students and their families understand that hidden costs exist, and that they may prove problematic. Fill out a more comprehensive checklist, and be wary of listed prices that seem too low. Understand just how complicated the financial aid process is.

paragraphs.label: L
paragraphs.text: Students and families must also understand their ability to self-advocate. They should not pay student bills or excess fees blindly. If something does not look right, ask about it. If it still doesn't look right, negotiate it. In cases where parents are working multiple jobs, are less knowledgeable about college bureaucracies, have limited English language skills, or are not contributing financially to their child's education, the burden of self-advocacy will fall on the student. I understand the difficulty, and the embarrassment. But it is necessary.

paragraphs.label: M
paragraphs.text: In the grand scheme of things, however, colleges also must come to understand that the hidden fees they ask for may prove unmanageable for the very kinds of low-income or first-generation students they are trying desperately to attract.

paragraphs.text: To write his 2010 book, The 5-Factor World Diet, nutritionist Harley Pasternak traveled to the healthiest countries around the world to learn more about what made their meals extra nourishing.

He noted that Japanese people ate a wonderful variety of seaweeds, and that Chinese people tried to include at least five different colors in every meal. Pasternak also came away with some valuable observations about how different the North American way of life was, compared with many other countries.

For starters, Americans eat much bigger portions than people in other countries. "We don't prioritize eating seasonally or locally, and we also add lots of salt, sugar and thickening agents to our foods," explained Pasternak. Contrast that to the healthy Mediterranean, Nordic and Okinawan diets listed in Pasternak's book. They all seem to stick to the ethos(特质) of regional, seasonal produce.

For example, a traditional Mediterranean diet includes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts and olive oil as the main components of nutritional intake. Fish, chicken and red wine make moderate appearances, while red meat, salt and sugar are used much less often. The benefits of a traditional Mediterranean diet have been studied since the 1970s, and researchers have found that living that olive oil life can help people lose weight, lower their heart disease risk and reverse diabetes.

Most other healthy eating cultures also make meals an event—say, multiple courses around the family table, or a glass or two of red wine at a long lunch—as opposed to hastily wolfing down handfuls of cereal above the kitchen sink and calling it dinner.

Each of the healthy eating cultures has its own unique feature. But Pasternak did take note of one unifying factor in all of the healthy societies he observed. "The only overlapping feature in most of these healthy countries is that they all walk way more than the average American," said Pasternak, "So really, regardless of what you're eating, if someone's walking four miles more than you each day, they're going to be a lot thinner and live a lot longer than you."

paragraphs.text: Recognizing when a friend or colleague feels sad, angry or surprised is key to getting along with others. But a new study suggests that being sensitive to people's feelings may sometimes come with an extra dose of stress. This and other research challenge the prevailing view that emotional intelligence is uniformly beneficial to its bearer.

In a study, psychologist Myriam Bechtoldt of the Frankfurt School of Finance and Management in Germany asked 166 male university students a series of questions to measure their emotional intelligence. For example, they showed the students photographs of people's faces and asked them to what extent feelings such as happiness or disgust were being expressed. The students then had to give job talks in front of judges who displayed serious facial expressions. The scientists measured concentrations of stress hormones in the students' saliva(唾液) before and after the talk.

In students who were rated more emotionally intelligent, the stress measures increased more during the experiment and took longer to go back to baseline. The findings suggest that some people may be too emotionally clever for their own good, says Bechtoldt. "Sometimes you can be so good at something that it causes trouble," she notes.

Indeed, the study adds to previous research hinting at a dark side of emotional intelligence. A study published in 2002 in Personality and Individual Differences suggested that emotionally perceptive people might be particularly influenced by feelings of depression and hopelessness. Furthermore, several studies have implied that emotional intelligence can be used to manipulate others for personal gains.

More research is needed to see how exactly the relation between emotional intelligence and stress would play out in women and in people of different ages and education levels. Nevertheless, emotional intelligence is a useful skill to have, as long as you learn to also properly cope with emotions—both others' and your own, says Bechtoldt. For example, some sensitive individuals may assume responsibility for other people's sadness or anger, which ultimately stresses them out. Remember, as Bechtoldt says, "you are not responsible for how other people feel."

在一项研究中，德国法兰克福金融与管理学院的心理学家 Myriam Bechtoldt 向 166 名男
大学生提了一系列问题，以测量他们的情商。
【选项】A) 偷换概念
To define different types of human feelings.意为「定义不同种类的人类情绪」，但
原文they showed the students photographs of people's faces and asked them to
what extent feelings such as happiness or disgust were being expressed.中「看脸
辨情绪」是测量情商的手段细节，不是研究目的。
B) ✓ 正确
to measure their emotional intelligence ↔ To assess the impacts of being emotionally clever
The findings suggest that some people may be too emotionally clever for their own good ↔
the impacts of being emotionally clever
定位句给出的是研究手段（测量情商加测压力激素），而P1与P3共同指明，这一手段服
务于「评估情商高带来的影响」这一目的，与B完全对应。
C) 无中生有
To demonstrate how to distinguish different feelings.意为「演示如何区分不同情
绪」，但实验是测量学生情商，不是教学生区分情绪；原文没有 demonstrate / teach
类动词。
D) 无中生有
To identify gender differences in emotional intelligence.说研究目的是识别性别差
异，但实验对象是166 male university students——全是男生，根本没设性别对照；
末段还提到More research is needed to see how exactly the relation between
emotional intelligence and stress would play out in women——女性差异是「待研
究」，不是本研究的目的。

questions.stem: What does the finding of Myriam Bechtoldt's study indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater emotional cleverness means less trouble in one's life.

options.label: B
options.text: Emotional intelligence helps people succeed in job interviews.

options.label: C
options.text: People's psychological wellbeing is related to various factors.

options.label: D
options.text: People may suffer from having a high emotional intelligence

questions.explanation:
【答案】D （细节题）
【判型】What does the finding of Myriam Bechtoldt's study indicate?问的是研究结果所「表
明」的内容，原文有研究者亲口下的结论句作为依据，仍属细节题，不需要超出原文做
推断。
【拆句】Q53结构是 What does + 主语 + indicate？主语the finding of Myriam Bechtoldt's
study由 of 介宾限定，全句是简单宾语从句式提问，无否定无比较，无陷阱。
【定位】The findings suggest that some people may be too emotionally clever for their own good,
says Bechtoldt.
研究者 Bechtoldt 说，研究结果表明，有些人的情商可能高过头反害了自己。
【选项】A) 与原文相反
Greater emotional cleverness means less trouble in one's life.说情商越高麻烦越
少，与原文Sometimes you can be so good at something that it causes trouble完
全相反。
B) 无中生有
Emotional intelligence helps people succeed in job interviews.说情商帮人在求职面
试中成功——但原文里give job talks in front of judges只是实验任务场景（求职演
讲），原文从未说情商高能让人面试成功；恰恰相反，情商高的人压力更大。
C) 答非所问
People's psychological wellbeing is related to various factors.「心理健康与多种因
素有关」在常识上无可指摘，但原文研究只讲情商与压力的关系，没有讨论「多种因
素」，是模糊化的万能选项。
D) ✓ 正确
some people may be too emotionally clever for their own good ↔
People may suffer from having a high emotional intelligence
Sometimes you can be so good at something that it causes trouble ↔
suffer from having a high emotional intelligence
预判「情商高反受其害」与People may suffer from having a high emotional
intelligence在主语、谓语、宾语三层完全咬合，且都保留 may 的不确定语气，是定位
句的标准同义改写。

questions.stem: What do we learn about emotional intelligence from a number of studies?

options.label: A
options.text: People suffering from depression are emotionally immature.

options.label: B
options.text: People who look at the dark side of life often feel depressed.

options.label: C
options.text: Some people may take advantage of it and benefit themselves.

options.label: D
options.text: Some people may lack it and are easily manipulated by others.

questions.explanation:
【答案】C （细节题）
【判型】What do we learn about emotional intelligence from a number of studies?问的是
「从多项研究我们得知什么」，对应原文综述段的事实罗列，不是推断或主旨。
【拆句】Q54主干是 What do we learn? 后接 about + 话题 + from + 来源两个介宾短语限定
learn 的范围；about 限定话题、from 限定信息来源，两个限定都不能丢，结构清晰、无
陷阱。
【定位】Furthermore, several studies have implied that emotional intelligence can be used to
manipulate others for personal gains.
此外，多项研究还暗示，情商可被用来操纵他人以谋取私利。
【选项】A) 张冠李戴
People suffering from depression are emotionally immature.说抑郁者情绪不成熟
——但原文emotionally perceptive people might be particularly influenced by
feelings of depression and hopelessness说的是「情绪敏锐者更易受抑郁影响」，主
语和因果都被改了。
B) 偷换概念
People who look at the dark side of life often feel depressed.说「看人生消极面的
人常抑郁」——这是日常常识，但原文谈的是「情绪敏锐者易受抑郁情绪影响」，主语
错配、因果也错。
C) ✓ 正确
emotional intelligence can be used to manipulate others for personal gains ↔
Some people may take advantage of it and benefit themselves
预判的「情商可被用来操纵他人谋私」与Some people may take advantage of it and
benefit themselves在主语、动词短语、目的三段完全对位，且 may 与 can 都是表
「可能性」的弱情态，无超译。
D) 与原文相反
Some people may lack it and are easily manipulated by others.说「有些人缺乏情
商，因此易被他人操纵」——但原文谈的是「情商高的人可以操纵别人」，而不是「缺
情商的人被人操纵」，施事与受事正好反过来。

questions.stem: What does the author suggest sensitive individuals do?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid burdening themselves with others' feelings.

options.label: B
options.text: Rid themselves of worries over worldly affairs.

options.label: C
options.text: Learn to cope with people's negative feelings.

options.label: D
options.text: Help people to deal with their troubles in life.

questions.explanation:
【答案】A （细节题）
【判型】What does the author suggest sensitive individuals do?问作者给敏感者的具体建议，
原文应有明示的建议句作为依据。
【拆句】Q55是 What does + 主语 + suggest + 宾语从句的疑问句；宾语从句省略 that，形式为
sensitive individuals do——主语 sensitive individuals + 动词原形 do，是 suggest sb.
(should) do 的虚拟语气省略式，do 表「做（什么）」，对应选项里的动词短语。
【定位】For example, some sensitive individuals may assume responsibility for other people's sadness
or anger, which ultimately stresses them out. Remember, as Bechtoldt says, "you are not
responsible for how other people feel."
举例来说，一些敏感的人可能会替别人的悲伤或愤怒揽责任，结果反而把自己压垮。记住
Bechtoldt 的话：你不必为别人的感受负责。
【选项】A) ✓ 正确
you are not responsible for how other people feel ↔
Avoid burdening themselves with others' feelings
some sensitive individuals may assume responsibility for other people's sadness or anger, which
ultimately stresses them out
↔ burdening themselves with others' feelings
预判的「别替别人的情绪扛锅」与Avoid burdening themselves with others' feelings
在动词、宾语、隐含主语三层完全对位，且都保留「避免、不要」的建议口吻。
B) 无中生有
Rid themselves of worries over worldly affairs.说「摆脱对世俗琐事的忧虑」——
但原文谈的是「别人的情绪」，不是「世俗琐事」；worldly affairs 在原文完全没有
对应。
C) 偷换概念
Learn to cope with people's negative feelings.建议敏感者去「应对他人的负面情
绪」——但原文you are not responsible for how other people feel给的建议恰恰相
反：「不必为别人感受负责」，根本不主张主动去处理别人的情绪。要注意原文确实有
learn to also properly cope with emotions—both others' and your own，但那是
给所有人的总建议、且强调「包括自己的」；针对 sensitive individuals 的针对性建议
是 not responsible 这一句。
D) 与原文相反
Help people to deal with their troubles in life.建议敏感者去「帮别人解决生活中的麻
烦」——这与作者的建议方向完全相反，作者明示you are not responsible for how
other people feel。

In this study, his team "went the  [29]  direction" by spending years carrying out individual interviews and group surveys to see what people really talk about when they talk about success.

As a scientist, Smith  [30]  studied individuality for a living, and even he was surprised to find younger respondents cared more about having a  [31]  in life. Perhaps this is because older people had fewer options when they were starting their careers, at a time when values focused more on stable incomes than  [32]  personal missions.

Other trends included an emphasis on the importance of parenting. Being a parent  [33]  very high across the priorities of all study participants. Ultimately, Smith hopes institutions will take note of these insights  [34]  .

Higher education institutions tend to focus on preparing students for high-paying jobs. For such institutions, from universities to workplaces, to better  [35]  people in the U.S., they'll need to understand "what the American public highly prioritizes," Smith says.

questions.stem: 第 26 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】E) fortune
名词
【词性槽】fame and ＿＿：and 并列一个名词
【依据】fame and fortune＝名利，是固定搭配
fame and fortune（名与利）是英语里押头韵的经典固定搭配。句意是“92% 的人认为别人
最看重名和利”，fortune＝财富，与 fame 并列恰成“名利”，且呼应全文“公众以为成功＝名
利、实则不然”的对比主旨。
【竞争词】J) profession “职业”与 fame 不构成习惯并列
profession 是“职业”，fame and profession 不是惯用搭配，也偏离“别人只在乎名利”这层
意思。
K) purpose 正话反说，purpose 属“真实成功观”，留给 31
purpose（人生意义）恰恰是文中人们“自己”真正看重的东西，与“别人只看重 fame and …”的语
境唱反调；它是 31 空 having a __(31)__ in life 的答案，留着它。

questions.stem: 第 27 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】M) released
动词
【词性槽】newly 与 study 之间缺过去分词作定语
【依据】“新近发布的研究”是固定说法
研究/报告与“发布”搭配：a newly released study＝一项新近发布的研究，正好接上一句结
论的来源 This is according to the newly __(27)__ study。release a study 是学术语境里
的常见表达。
【竞争词】C) acquiring -ing 主动义，与 study 不搭
acquiring 是现在分词，表“正在获得……的”主动义，study 不会主动去“获得”什么，a newly
acquiring study 讲不通。
D) bothered 词义不对，研究不会“被困扰”
bothered 意为“被困扰的”，a newly bothered study（新近被困扰的研究）语义荒谬，与“发布
研究”的语境完全无关。
F) fulfilling 义为“充实的”，且后面 28 题更需要它
fulfilling 表“令人有成就感的”，修饰 study 不通；且它在下文 32 空有更贴的去处，留着它。

a newly ranked study（新近被排名的研究）不通，ranked 表“排名、位列”，是 33 空 Being a

questions.stem: 第 28 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】D) bothered
动词
【词性槽】was ＿＿ by：被动结构里的过去分词
【依据】was bothered by＝被……所困扰/感到不安
be bothered by 是固定搭配，意为“被……困扰、对……感到不安”。Smith 对过去研
究“assumed what people will care about”（想当然地假设人们在乎什么）这一做法感到
不满/困扰，正是他另起炉灶做新研究的动机，与下句 his team "went the __(29)__
direction"（走相反方向）顺理成章地衔接。

questions.stem: 第 29 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】I) opposite
名词
【词性槽】the ＿＿ direction：the 与 direction 间作定语的名词
【依据】the opposite direction＝相反的方向
go the opposite direction＝“走相反的方向”，正好承接上句 Smith 对旧研究“想当然假设”
的不满 he was __(28)__ by how past studies ...——所以他的团队反其道而行，by
spending years carrying out individual interviews and group surveys to see what
people really talk about，用实地访谈去问人们真正在乎什么。opposite 在此作定语修

questions.stem: 第 30 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】H) literally
副词
【词性槽】主语与动词 studied 之间插一个状语
【依据】literally 强调“确确实实、名副其实地”
Smith 是研究个体差异的科学家，literally studied individuality for a living＝“确实是以研
究个体差异为生”，literally 在这里起强调作用，凸显“连研究这行的他都没料到”的转折，与
后半句 and even he was surprised 呼应。
【竞争词】B) accordingly 表“相应地”，无前因可承接
accordingly 意为“因此、据此”，需要前文有可据以行动的原因，这里只是陈述他的职业，用它
逻辑上接不上；它是 34 空的答案。
N) similarly 表“同样地”，需有可类比对象
similarly 表“与前述类似地”，需要前文有一个可对照的相似情形，此处没有，用它前后无可比
之处。

questions.stem: 第 31 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】K) purpose
名词
【词性槽】a ＿＿ in life：不定冠词 a 后接名词
【依据】have a purpose in life＝人生有目标/意义
have a purpose in life 是地道搭配，意为“人生有意义、有使命感”。下一句把它换说成
that prioritization 并与 stable incomes than __(32)__ personal missions（个人使命）呼
应——purpose 正是“personal mission”这层“人生意义”的概念，与全文“年轻人更看重人生
意义而非名利”的发现一致。
【竞争词】J) profession “职业”不与 in life 搭、也偏离主旨
a profession in life 不是惯用表达，且“有一份职业”讲的是谋生，与本段强调年轻人看重“人生意
义”而非稳定收入的对比相悖。

questions.stem: 第 32 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】F) fulfilling
形容词
【词性槽】＿＿ personal missions：名词短语前作定语
【依据】fulfilling＝令人有成就感的，与 missions 同向
fulfilling personal missions＝“令人充实／有成就感的个人使命”。本段对比的是“老一辈更
看重稳定收入 (stable incomes) vs 年轻人更看重有意义的个人使命”，fulfilling 这一正向、
表“成就感”的形容词，恰好刻画年轻人追求的那种“有意义的”使命，与 31 空 purpose 一脉
相承。
【竞争词】I) opposite “相反的”修饰 missions 语义不成立
opposite 表“相反的、对立的”，opposite personal missions（相反的个人使命）讲不通，且与

wrong 是“错误的”，带贬义；这里要正面描述年轻人向往的使命，用 wrong personal missions

【易错】最具迷惑性的错误词是 O) —— wrong 词性对、又被开头“误解”一词带偏。32 题 than
__(32)__ personal missions 处，wrong 是形容词、能修饰 missions，加上首句 might be
totally misguided 谈“错误认知”，容易让人顺手填“wrong”。防坑：本空要正面描述年轻人

questions.stem: 第 33 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】L) ranked
动词
【词性槽】主语 Being a parent 之后缺谓语动词
【依据】rank high＝排名靠前、位列很高
rank high 是固定搭配，意为“排名很高、位居前列”，正好接 very high：Being a parent
__(33)__ very high＝“为人父母在所有受访者的优先项里排得很高”，与上一句 Other

一脉相承。
【竞争词】C) acquiring -ing 形式不能单独作谓语
acquiring 是现在分词，单独不能充当谓语动词；且“获得很高”与 very high 也搭不上。

bothered 意为“困扰”，Being a parent bothered very high 既不通顺也无意义。
F) fulfilling 义为“充实的”，与 high 不搭，留给 32
fulfilling 是形容词“令人有成就感的”，不能跟 very high 构成“排名很高”，且它在 32 空有更贴
的位置。

questions.stem: 第 34 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】B) accordingly
副词
【词性槽】句末修饰动词短语 take note 的状语
【依据】据研究结论“相应地”采取行动
前文摆出研究发现（人们真正看重的是人生意义、为人父母等），Smith 希望机构 take
note of these insights accordingly＝“相应地、据此去关注这些洞见”，accordingly 承接
“根据上述发现 → 据此行动”的因果逻辑，与末段 they'll need to understand "what the
American public highly prioritizes" 的导向一致。
【竞争词】N) similarly 表“同样地”，缺可类比对象
similarly 需要前文给出一个相似情形来类比，这里是“据研究结论行动”的因果关系而非类比，用
它逻辑断裂。

questions.stem: 第 35 空
questions.explanation:
【答案】A) accommodate
动词
【词性槽】to better ＿＿ people：to 后跟动词原形
【依据】accommodate people＝顾及、服务好人群的需求
末段说机构要了解 "what the American public highly prioritizes"（美国公众最看重什
么），目的是 to better accommodate people＝“更好地顾及/迁就人们（的真实需
求）”，accommodate 在此为“适应、满足某群体需求”，与“先懂公众所重、再据此服务好
他们”的逻辑严丝合缝。
【竞争词】G) identify 义为“识别”，与“服务好人们”指向不符

【易错】最具迷惑性的错误词是 G) —— identify 词性全对、也能接 people，最易误选。35 题 to
better __(35)__ people in the U.S. 处，identify 与正确答案 accommodate 同为及物动
词、宾语都能是 people，光看语法分不开。防坑：回到句子目的——机构是“懂了公众所重

切开两词。

title: 2022年09月真题·第1套 · 长篇匹配（How a rabbit study and a）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At whatever grade level teachers find themselves, from kindergarten to the final class at medical or law school, few moments stir the emotions as deeply as when former students reappear years and often decades later with an update on where their journey has taken them and what resiliencies(韧性) have been the pavement on which they've traveled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: So it was when a recent letter came from Kelli Harding, a student 21 years ago in my Peace Studies summer course in Washington. The weekly tuition-free class, in a roomy space that Ralph Nader and his Public Citizen nonprofit group provided, was discussion-based and required no useless homework or exams. Just come in and figure out how to increase peace and decrease violence. And do it today, tomorrow is too late. The course attracted mostly congressional interns(实习生), with a few exceptions like Kelli who was in Washington as an AmeriCorps volunteer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Her year-long service included comforting AIDS patients at a free health clinic and delivering meals to the homebound. It was a world apart from her undergraduate days at the University of California-Berkeley majoring in political science. The Washington experience, which Kelli would later call "transformative", was the fuel that carried her into medicine to earn a master's degree in public health from Columbia University and a medical degree from the University of Rochester, and almost two decades of practice as an emergency-room psychiatrist(精神科医生) at New York-Presbyterian Hospital and a clinical professor of psychiatry at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kelli's letter, a literate update on both her personal and professional life, touched my heart, and especially so when saying that two decades later she still has the course text, "Solutions to Violence," and that "it remains one of my favorite possessions." She lives in Lower Manhattan with her husband, Padraic, whom she met on a flight to London, and their three boys.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If Kelli stands out, it's because she is also a gifted writer. Last month, Atria Books published her book The Rabbit Effect: Live Longer, Happier, and Healthier with the Groundbreaking Science of Kindness.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: With a blending of free-flowing confessional prose and scholarly research found in 461 notes, Kelli met my expectations that her ideas and ideals would be sound and singular. "Despite our scientific progress," she writes, "Americans are remarkably unhealthy. In 2016, the United States ranked forty-third in the world for life expectancy. It is also by far the world's most expensive place to get sick."

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Enter the rabbits—not those running around in our woodlands but ones serving in two month-long medical experiments to test the effects of eating a high-fat diet and the connections between cholesterol and heart disease. With similar diets, the expectations were that all the rabbits would have similar cloggings of their arteries(动脉堵塞). Yet one group had 60% fewer of them.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The reason? Instead of receiving the standard care given to lab animals, the 60% group was watched over by a newcomer to the lab who, Kelli writes, "handled the animals differently. When she fed her rabbits she talked to them and petted them. She didn't just pass out food, she gave them love. The studies indicate something is missing in the traditional biomedical model. It wasn't diet or genetics that made a difference in which rabbits got sick and which stayed healthy. It was kindness."

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Amid the political noise about Obamacare, Medicare, Medicaid, health insurance and thieving pharmaceutical(医药的) companies, Kelli Harding stands apart from the crowd calling for quick fixes, the simpler the better. She has walked too many miles in the halls of hospitals visiting too many far-gone patients and seeing too many medical mistakes to go along with conventional thinking.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: "The rabbit effect," she explains, means that "when it comes to our health, we've been missing some crucial pieces: hidden factors behind what really makes us healthy. Factors like love, friendship, and dignity. The designs of our neighborhoods, schools, and workplaces. There's a social dimension to health that we've completely overlooked in our efforts to find the best and most cutting-edge medical care … Ultimately, what affects our health in the most meaningful ways has more to do with how we treat one another, how we live, and how we think about what it means to be human than with anything that happens in the doctor's office."

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: In more than a few passages, she relates the stories of men and women who came up against assembly-line medicine where patients were treated mostly as pieces of flesh. "Clinically," she writes, "it's common to see two patients with the same condition, such as recovering from a heart attack, have two very different courses based on seemingly irrelevant factors, such as their family relationships or their educational levels. In my practice, the sickest people I see often share similar backgrounds: loneliness, abuse, poverty, or discrimination. For them, the medical model isn't enough. It's like fixing up an airplane engine and ignoring that the pilot is on his third drink at the bar and a massive storm is overhead … To properly care for patients, we also need to care about the lives of the people getting the care."

paragraphs.label: L
paragraphs.text: Kelli wastes no time taking potshots at(随意批评) the medical establishment and its body-centered biomedicine methods. Instead, she remains positive, holding up for praise one of her medical school professors, George Engel, "who always noticed not just a patient's physical condition but little details about her life, such as if she had family pictures up in her hospital room or flowers delivered. He was the kind of trusted doctor you'd feel relieved to see and welcome into the room with a sick family member. He'd sit down to talk with the patient not just about medical problems, but about her life and priorities. He built a large consultation service to address the holistic(整体的) needs of hospitalized patients, including psychological and social factors."

paragraphs.label: M
paragraphs.text: It's a guess how many George Engels in their white jackets are at work these days and another speculation on the number of Kelli Hardings the nation is blessed with. May the totals be large and getting larger.
